Let M be a closed manifold of even dimension n=2m, with a Riemannian metric and a spin structure. Let S=S+⊕S− be its spinor bundle, and let W be a Hermitian vector bundle with a unitary connection of vector-bundle curvature FW=(∇W)2. We use Clifford multiplication satisfying c(v)c(w)+c(w)c(v)=−2⟨v,w⟩, so the Twisted Dirac operator
DW​=∑i​c(ei)∇ei​S⊗W​=(0DW+​​DW−​0​)
(1)
is self-adjoint and DW−​=(DW+​)∗. Here (ei​) is an oriented local orthonormal basis and (ei) its dual. The Atiyah-Singer index theorem in this setting is
indDW+​=∫M​[A(RTM)∧trexp(2πiFW​)]2m​.​
(2)
The second factor is the Chern character; the first is the A-hat form
A(R)=det1/2(sinh(R/(4πi))R/(4πi)​).
(3)
The square root has constant term one. All functions of the vector-bundle curvature matrices mean power series truncated above the dimension of M. The brackets select the top-degree differential form. The Bianchi identity shows that these forms are closed, and Chern-Weil connection transgression shows that their de Rham cohomology classes do not depend on the chosen connections on a vector bundle.
The global step is supersymmetric quantum mechanics. On the Hilbert space L2(S⊗W), take the grading operator Γ, the odd supercharge DW​, and the nonnegative Hamiltonian H=DW2​. They obey ΓDW​=−DW​Γ and DW2​=H. The principal symbol of DW​ is invertible away from the zero covector, so elliptic regularity and Rellich-Kondrachov compactness theorem give a smooth discrete orthonormal eigenbasis for H, finite-dimensional eigenspaces, and a trace-class operator e−tH for t>0. Define its supertrace by StrA=Tr(ΓA).
For every positive eigenvalue λ of H, the map λ−1/2DW​ is an isomorphism between its positive and negative grading eigenspaces, with inverse itself. Their contributions to the supertrace cancel. The zero eigenspaces are kerDW+​ and kerDW−​. Consequently
Stre−tDW2​=dimkerDW+​−dimkerDW−​=indDW+​(t>0).
(4)
This also proves independence of t without differentiating an unbounded operator inside a trace. If Kt​ is the heat kernel, the heat kernel trace formula gives
indDW+​=∫M​strS⊗W​Kt​(x,x)dvolg​(x).
(5)
The remaining task is to compute this local integrand as t↓0.
Fix p∈M, use geodesic normal coordinates x, and trivialize S⊗W by radial parallel transport. Expanding DW2​ at p gives the Lichnerowicz formula for a twisted Dirac operator:
DW2​=∇∗∇+41​Scal+∑i<j​c(ei)c(ej)FijW​.
(6)
Indeed the terms with identical indices give the rough Laplacian. The other terms are ∑i<j​c(ei)c(ej)[∇i​,∇j​]. Decompose this vector-bundle curvature into spin curvature and FW; substituting the spin curvature into the Clifford algebra relations and the algebraic Bianchi identity leaves Scal/4. Thus the calculation retains the curvature of the twisting bundle explicitly.
There is an especially strong cancellation in the spinor supertrace. With Γ=imc(e1)⋯c(e2m), every ordered product of distinct Clifford generators of degree less than 2m has zero supertrace, while
strS​(c(e1)⋯c(e2m))=(−2i)m.
(7)
For an even product of lower degree, conjugate Γ times that product by a missing Clifford generator: it changes sign, so its matrix trace is zero. An odd product exchanges the grading summands and also has zero supertrace. For the full product, (c(e1)⋯c(e2m))2=(−1)m, and dimS=2m, giving the displayed constant.
To exploit this, identify the Clifford algebra as a filtered vector space with the exterior algebra by sending an ordered Clifford product to the corresponding wedge product of differential forms. Implement Getzler rescaling: put x=εy, t=ε2s, multiply the degree-k exterior component of the kernel by ε−k, and multiply the whole kernel by ε2m. A derivative and a Clifford generator have rescaling degree one; a coordinate has degree minus one. Clifford contractions lower the degree by two relative to the wedge product of differential forms, so the leading product becomes exterior multiplication.
In the radially parallel frame, the linear Taylor term of the connection is determined by its vector-bundle curvature: if Ai​ is its matrix, then Ai​(x)=21​xjFji​(p)+O(∣x∣2). To check the coefficient, radial gauge means xiAi​=0, and integration of xjFji​ along the radial segment gives Ai​(x)=∫01​sxjFji​(sx)ds. Combining this formula with the spin representation, the symmetries of Riemann curvature tensor, and the Lichnerowicz formula for a twisted Dirac operator, the rescaled square has leading model
Hp​=−∑i​(∂yi​​−41​∑j​Rij​yj​)2+FpW​.
(8)
Here R is the skew matrix of tangent-bundle curvature two-forms at p; changing the curvature-matrix sign convention changes the sign inside the covariant derivatives but not the determinant below. The coefficients act in ΛTp∗​M⊗End(Wp​). The scalar-curvature term has degree zero and disappears after multiplication by ε2; the linear spin-connection term and the Clifford action of FW have degree two and survive. Higher Taylor terms have smaller degree and disappear.
For clarity, the analytic meaning of this limiting calculation is the following. Construct the local heat kernel expansion to any fixed order and insert the Taylor expansion of the rescaled coefficients into its transport equations. At each exterior degree, the leading equation is the heat equation of Hp​; the remaining terms acquire positive powers of ε. Equivalently, successive substitutions in
e−sPε​−e−sHp​=−∫0s​e−(s−u)Pε​(Pε​−Hp​)e−uHp​du
(9)
give the same expansion. Polynomial spatial factors are integrable against the local Gaussian kernels, and only finitely many exterior degrees exist. A cutoff outside a fixed normal neighbourhood contributes O(e−c/t). Choosing the initial expansion order arbitrarily large bounds its differentiated remainder to any required order. This proves convergence of the rescaled diagonal kernel to the model diagonal kernel, uniformly in p on the compact manifold. Its degree-2m component has no net power of ε, precisely the component detected by the spinor supertrace.
We can compute the model kernel rather than invoke a local index formula. Set F=FpW​ and seek its kernel from the origin in the form
ks​(y,0)=a(s)exp(−41​yTQ(s)y)e−sF.
(10)
The scalar even exterior coefficients of R commute. On this ansatz the rotational first-order term vanishes because Q is a function of R2. Expanding the model operator gives −∑∂i2​+21​(Ry)⋅∇+161​yTR2y+F, so substitution into the heat equation gives
Q′=41​R2−Q2,aa′​=−21​trQ.
(11)
The Euclidean initial condition Q(s)∼s−1I, a(s)∼(4πs)−m selects
Q(s)=2R​coth(2sR​),a(s)=(4πs)−mdet1/2(sinh(sR/2)sR/2​).
(12)
These expressions have well-defined power series at R=0. This is the curvature version of the Gaussian calculation underlying the Mehler formula for Hermite functions.
At s=1, y=0, multiply the top exterior coefficient by the spinor supertrace constant. Since (4π)−m(−2i)m=(2πi)−m, and every curvature factor is a two-form, the result is
limt↓0​strKt​(p,p)dvolg​(p)=[det1/2(sinh(RTM/(4πi))RTM/(4πi)​)trexp(−2πiFW​)]2m​(p).
(13)
Integration and the constant supertrace established above prove the boxed Atiyah-Singer index theorem. The mechanism is that odd symmetry pairs the nonzero spectrum globally, while the Clifford filtration makes the surviving local contribution an explicitly solvable curvature oscillator. Odd-dimensional spin Dirac operators have no canonical chiral index of this type; their self-adjoint Fredholm index is zero. For comparison of normalization conventions, Raphaël Ponge's local index calculation writes the same unnormalized curvature model and spinor supertrace constant.

Use Tn=Rn/(2πZ)n and the periodic Sobolev space convention
∥f∥Hs2​=∑k∈Zn​(1+∣k∣2)s∣f​(k)∣2.
(14)
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives
∑k​∣f​(k)∣≤∥f∥Hs​(∑k​(1+∣k∣2)−s)1/2.
(15)
To check the last sum, partition the lattice into ∣k∣<1 and dyadic shells 2j≤∣k∣<2j+1. A shell contains at most Cn​2jn points and contributes at most Cn​2j(n−2s). This is a convergent geometric series exactly when s>n/2.
Thus the Fourier series ∑k​f​(k)eik⋅x converges absolutely and uniformly on the torus. Its sum is a continuous function and has the original Fourier coefficients, so it represents the original periodic distribution. In particular the representative is unique and
Hs(Tn)↪C(Tn),∥f∥∞​≤Cs,n​∥f∥Hs​(s>n/2).​
(16)
This proves the requested inclusion, with its continuous Sobolev embedding estimate.

b OurBigBook.com
Let V be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space, and let A⊆End(V) be a unital subalgebra stable under the adjoint operator. Define its commutant of an operator algebra by A′={T:Ta=aT for all a∈A}. The double commutant theorem for star-algebras asserts A′′=A​. The inclusion A⊆A′′ follows immediately from the definition; we prove the reverse.
Write N=dimV, fix a basis v1​,…,vN​, and act diagonally on VN. The linear subspace
W={(av1​,…,avN​):a∈A}
(17)
is invariant under every diagonal a. Since A is closed under adjoints, its orthogonal complement W⊥ is invariant too: ⟨aw,z⟩=⟨w,a∗z⟩=0 for w∈W⊥, z∈W. Hence the orthogonal projection P onto W commutes with every diagonal a.
Writing P as an N by N block matrix (Pij​), this says Pij​a=aPij​, so each Pij​∈A′. If b∈A′′, it commutes with every Pij​, and its diagonal action therefore commutes with P and preserves W. Because 1∈A, (v1​,…,vN​)∈W. Therefore there is one a∈A such that
(bv1​,…,bvN​)=(av1​,…,avN​).
(18)
Equality on the basis gives b=a, proving the theorem over either scalar field.
The identity hypothesis is necessary. For a possibly nonunital adjoint-stable subalgebra, adjoining the ambient identity does not change its commutant of an operator algebra, so the exact statement is A′′=A+FI. For example A={0} has A′′=FI on a nonzero V. Thus the usual exam formulation takes the algebra to contain the identity.

At a fixed t, write A=f(t) and B=f′(t). Differentiating the matrix exponential in the direction B gives
dtd​ef(t)=∫01​e(1−u)f(t)f′(t)euf(t)du.​
(19)
The order of factors matters because matrix multiplication need not be commutative.
To prove the derivative of the matrix exponential formula, expand its power series. The coefficient linear in h in (A+hB)k is ∑j=0k−1​AjBAk−1−j. On bounded sets of matrices, the exponential series and its directional derivative series converge uniformly: the latter is dominated in operator norm by ∥B∥∑k≥1​k∥A∥k−1/k!. Terms with two or more hB factors have sum O(h2) locally. Hence the derivative is
∑k≥1​k!1​∑j=0k−1​AjBAk−1−j.
(20)
On the other hand, the integral in the box expands absolutely as
∑a,b≥0​a!b!AaBAb​∫01​(1−u)aubdu=∑a,b≥0​(a+b+1)!AaBAb​.
(21)
The integral identity follows by repeated integration by parts. Grouping by a+b=k−1 gives the same derivative. Finally differentiability means f(t+h)=A+hB+o(h); the locally bounded derivative of the exponential sends the o(h) error to o(h), proving the chain rule even when f′ is not continuous. If [f,f′]=0, the formula simplifies to eff′.

Let e(ω) denote exterior multiplication, e(ω)α=ω∧α. For a q-form α, evaluation of the proposed operator on vector fields Y0​,…,Yq​ gives
(∑i​ωi​∧∇Xi​​α)(Y0​,…,Yq​)=∑a=0q​(−1)a(∇Ya​​α)(Y0​,…,Ya​,…,Yq​),
(22)
since ∑i​ωi​(Ya​)Xi​=Ya​. This expression is independent of the chosen local basis.
Expand each covariant derivative into the derivative of α(Y0​,…,Ya​,…,Yq​) minus the terms obtained by differentiating each argument. For every pair a<b, those argument terms combine into
(−1)a+bα(∇Ya​​Yb​−∇Yb​​Ya​,Y0​,…,Ya​,…,Yb​,…,Yq​).
(23)
The Levi-Civita connection is a torsion-free connection, so the vector in this expression is [Ya​,Yb​]. The result is exactly the defining evaluation formula for the exterior derivative:
(dα)(Y0​,…,Yq​)=∑a​(−1)aYa​(α(Y0​,…,Ya​,…,Yq​))+∑a<b​(−1)a+bα([Ya​,Yb​],Y0​,…,Ya​,…,Yb​,…,Yq​).
(24)
Therefore d=i∑​e(ωi​)∇Xi​​​. No orthonormality or compactness is needed for this identity; the dual-frame property and vanishing torsion tensor suffice.

Suppose first that the bounded Fredholm operator T:H→H has Fredholm index zero. Put N=kerT and C=(ranT)⊥=kerT∗. These finite-dimensional linear subspaces have the same dimension. The restricted map T:N⊥→ranT is a bounded bijection, with bounded inverse by the bounded inverse theorem. Choose an isomorphism J:N→C and extend it by zero on N⊥, writing the resulting finite-rank operator as K.
Relative to the orthogonal decompositions H=N⊕N⊥ and H=C⊕ranT, the operator T+K is the direct sum of J and the invertible restricted map. Thus T+K is invertible, and T=(T+K)−K is the sum of an invertible operator and a compact operator.
Conversely write T=U+K with U invertible and K compact. It suffices to treat I+C with C=U−1K. A compact operator on a Hilbert space admits arbitrary operator norm approximation by finite-rank operators: take a finite epsilon-net of its unit-ball image and project onto the span of the net. Choose F of finite rank with ∥C−F∥<1, put R=C−F, and factor
I+C=(I+R)(I+(I+R)−1F).
(25)
The first factor is invertible by the Neumann series. Set G=(I+R)−1F and E=ranG, a finite-dimensional linear subspace. On E⊕E⊥, the second factor has block form
I+G=(A0​BI​),A=IE​+G∣E​.
(26)
Left multiplication by the invertible block matrix (I0​−BI​) reduces it to A⊕I. Its range is closed, and its kernel and cokernel have equal dimension by finite-dimensional rank-nullity theorem for A:E→E. Invertible factors preserve all these properties. Hence T is a Fredholm operator of Fredholm index zero, proving both directions:
T Fredholm with index 0⟺T=U+K,U invertible, K compact.​
(27)

The Clifford algebra relation implies
[C(a)C(b),C(v)]=2(b,v)C(a)−2(a,v)C(b).
(28)
Indeed move C(v) past C(b) and then past C(a) using the two anticommutator identities; the three-generator products cancel.
Since all C(w) are self-adjoint,
π(T)∗+π(T)=41​∑i​(C(ei​)C(Tei​)+C(Tei​)C(ei​))=21​∑i​(ei​,Tei​)I=0.
(29)
Each scalar vanishes because T is skew-adjoint. This proves π(T)∗=−π(T)​.
For the requested commutator, the first identity gives
[π(T),C(v)]=21​∑i​((ei​,v)C(Tei​)−(Tei​,v)C(ei​)).
(30)
The first sum is C(Tv) by the orthonormal basis expansion of v. For the second, the skew-adjoint property gives ∑i​(Tei​,v)ei​=−Tv. By real linearity of C, the difference is therefore
[π(T),C(v)]=21​(C(Tv)−C(−Tv))=C(Tv).​
(31)
This calculation explains the factor 1/4: it makes infinitesimal rotations of V act correctly on its Clifford generators.

Products below combine matrix multiplication with the wedge product of differential forms of differential forms. Differentiate the projection identity p2=p to get
(dp)p+pdp=dp,pdp=dp(1−p)​.
(32)
Multiplying by p on both sides also gives pdpp=0; applying the same argument to 1−p gives (1−p)dp(1−p)=0. Thus at each point dp is off-diagonal relative to imp⊕kerp, whereas (dp)2 is diagonal and commutes with p. For ω=p(dp)2,
ωk=p(dp)2k(k≥1),dω=(dp)3,
(33)
because d(dp)=0.
The graded Leibniz rule and cyclicity of the matrix trace give, since ω has even degree,
dtr(ωk)=ktr((dω)ωk−1).
(34)
Here (dω)ωk−1 is off-diagonal: (dp)3 is off-diagonal and every power of ω is diagonal. Its matrix trace is zero. Hence dtr(ωk)=0​ for every k≥1; for k=0 the trace is the constant matrix size.
For the determinant, work over the commutative algebra of even differential forms. If f(0)=1, write f(ω)=I+N, where N has strictly positive degree and is nilpotent for dimensional reasons. The finite power series identity
detf(ω)=exp(trlog(I+N)),log(I+N)=∑j≥1​j(−1)j+1​Nj
(35)
holds over this algebra, as follows either from the formal determinant identity over characteristic-zero commutative rings or by differentiating det(I+sN) in the scalar variable s. Each Nj is a linear combination of positive powers of ω. The matrix trace of the logarithm is therefore a closed differential form, and its finite exponential is closed by the graded Leibniz rule. Thus ddetf(ω)=0​. The projection connection interprets ω as the curvature of pd on imp, but the proof above directly establishes both closedness claims.

The positive sign printed in the exponential uses the skew-adjoint convention for the Dirac operator: D∗=−D, so D−​=−D+∗​. Put A=D+​ and define the nonnegative self-adjoint operators
P=A∗A=−D−​D+​,Q=AA∗=−D+​D−​.
(36)
For t>0, the assumed compact elliptic spectral theorem for these elliptic differential operators gives discrete eigenvalues, finite multiplicities and trace-class operators e−tP, e−tQ.
If Pu=λu with λ>0, then Q(Au)=A(Pu)=λAu and Au=0. Conversely A∗ sends the λ eigenspace of Q to that of P. On these eigenspaces the inverse of A is λ−1A∗. Thus the positive spectra agree with multiplicity, and absolute convergence of the operator traces permits cancellation term by term:
Tre−tP−Tre−tQ=dimkerP−dimkerQ=dimkerA−dimkerA∗.
(37)
The last expression is the Fredholm index of A, since its closed range has orthogonal complement kerA∗. Consequently
indD+​=Tr(etD−​D+​)−Tr(etD+​D−​),t>0.​
(38)
This is the supertrace cancellation used in Question 1. If the Dirac operator is instead defined to be self-adjoint, D−​=(D+​)∗ and the heat exponentials must have a minus sign. With that convention the positive exponentials in the printed formula are generally unbounded and have no finite operator trace.

Interpret H−∞​(Tn)=⋃s∈R​Hs(Tn), the periodic distributions of finite negative Sobolev space order. Smooth multiplication is bounded on every periodic Sobolev space. One direct proof uses the rapid decay of the Fourier coefficients of V: the inequality
⟨k⟩s≤Cs​⟨k−ℓ⟩∣s∣⟨ℓ⟩s,⟨k⟩=(1+∣k∣2)1/2,
(39)
reduces the weighted convolution formula for Vf​ to an ℓ1∗ℓ2 estimate. Thus ∥Vf∥Hs​≤CV,s​∥f∥Hs​ for every real s.
Suppose initially f∈Hs. The equation gives Δf=u−Vf∈Hs, since a smooth function belongs to every periodic Sobolev space. For k=0, the Fourier multiplier of Δ is ∣k∣2, and
(1+∣k∣2)s+2∣f​(k)∣2≤4(1+∣k∣2)s∣Δf​(k)∣2.
(40)
The zero coefficient is already finite. Hence f∈Hs+2. Iterating the argument gives f∈Hs+2j for every j≥0. Applying the Sobolev embedding theorem also to each distributional partial derivative produces a smooth representative. Therefore f∈C∞(Tn)​. This is an explicit elliptic regularity bootstrap, valid for complex or real V and without a sign assumption on it.

Every entire holomorphic function has a Taylor series f(z)=∑n≥0​an​zn, uniformly convergent on each circle. Angular orthogonality gives
2π1​∫02π​∣f(reiθ)∣2dθ=∑n≥0​∣an​∣2r2n.
(41)
Integrate in polar coordinates and use Tonelli theorem for the nonnegative sum:
∥f∥F2​=2∑n≥0​∣an​∣2∫0∞​r2n+1e−r2dr=∑n≥0​n!∣an​∣2.
(42)
The last integral equals n!/2 by substituting u=r2 and repeated integration by parts.
Conversely, for any (bn​)∈ℓ2, set an​=bn​/n!​. On ∣z∣≤R, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives
∑n≥0​∣an​zn∣≤(∑n​∣bn​∣2)1/2(∑n​n!R2n​)1/2=∥(bn​)∥ℓ2​eR2/2.
(43)
Applied to the tails, the same bound proves uniform convergence on every disk. The series therefore defines an entire holomorphic function, and the norm identity puts it in the Bargmann-Fock space F. The coefficient map f↦(n!​an​) is consequently an onto linear isometry F→ℓ2; polarization also identifies the inner products. Completeness of ℓ2 proves that F is a Hilbert space. Its standard coordinate orthonormal basis corresponds to
en​(z)=n!​zn​,n=0,1,….​
(44)
The norm identity shows both their unit norms and completeness; it also gives ∣f(z)∣≤e∣z∣2/2∥f∥F​.

To distinguish the two normalizations, denote the physicists' Hermite polynomial by hn​(x)=(−1)nex2(d/dx)ne−x2. Define the normalized Hermite functions by
Hn​(x)=π1/42nn!​hn​(x)e−x2/2​.​
(45)
Introduce the differential operators a=(x+d/dx)/2​, a∗=(x−d/dx)/2​ on the Schwartz space. Direct multiplication gives [a,a∗]=1 and
−d2/dx2+x2=2a∗a+1.
(46)
The Gaussian H0​=π−1/4e−x2/2 satisfies aH0​=0, and repeated differentiation gives Hn​=(a∗)nH0​/n!​. The commutator identity implies aHn​=n​Hn−1​ and a∗Hn​=n+1​Hn+1​. Therefore
(−d2/dx2+x2)Hn​=(2n+1)Hn​.​
(47)
For normalization, integration by parts makes a∗ the adjoint operator of a on these rapidly decreasing functions, so ∥(a∗)nH0​∥2=n!∥H0​∥2=n!. Distinct eigenvalues of the symmetric quantum harmonic oscillator give orthogonality.
The generating identity follows directly from the Rodrigues definition of the Hermite polynomials:
∑n≥0​n!hn​(x)​wn=ex2∑n≥0​n!(−w)n​(d/dx)ne−x2=ex2e−(x−w)2=e2xw−w2.
(48)
The Taylor expansion of the entire Gaussian justifies the middle equality for every complex w. Substitute w=z/2​ and the Bargmann-Fock space basis en​(z)=zn/n!​ to obtain
n≥0∑​Hn​(x)en​(z)=Ax​(z):=π−1/4e−x2/2+2​xz−z2/2.​
(49)
The convergence is locally uniform in z by the same entire generating series.
For 0<t<1, Ax​(t​z) belongs to the Bargmann-Fock space: after writing z=u+iv, its squared modulus times e−∣z∣2 has strictly negative quadratic coefficients −(1+t)u2−(1−t)v2. Taking the Bargmann-Fock space inner product of the two generating functions and using the orthonormal basis proved in part (b) gives
∑n≥0​tnHn​(x)Hn​(y)=π1​∫C​Ax​(t​z)Ay​(t​z)​e−∣z∣2dudv.
(50)
The coefficient series converges absolutely by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Substitution factors the right side into
π3/2e−(x2+y2)/2​∫R​e−(1+t)u2+2t​(x+y)udu∫R​e−(1−t)v2+i2t​(x−y)vdv.
(51)
Use the Gaussian integral ∫e−au2+budu=π/a​eb2/(4a) for a>0 and complex b; the complex case follows from the real case by analyticity. The resulting exponent is
−2x2+y2​+2(1+t)t(x+y)2​−2(1−t)t(x−y)2​=2(1−t2)4xyt−(1+t2)(x2+y2)​.
(52)
Thus the Mehler formula for Hermite functions is
n≥0∑​tnHn​(x)Hn​(y)=π(1−t2)​1​exp(2(1−t2)4xyt−(1+t2)(x2+y2)​).​
(53)
As a normalization check, its t↓0 limit is H0​(x)H0​(y). Setting t=e−2s and multiplying by e−s yields the harmonic oscillator transition kernel with eigenvalues 2n+1.

d OurBigBook.com
For a closed manifold M with an oriented Riemannian metric, define δ to be the formal L2 adjoint operator of the exterior derivative, equivalently δ=(−1)n(q+1)+1∗d∗ on q-forms. The Hodge Laplacian is Δq​=dδ+δd. The Hodge decomposition theorem states that its space Hq=kerΔq​ of harmonic differential forms is finite-dimensional and smooth, and that
Ωq(M)=Hq⊕⊥dΩq−1(M)⊕⊥δΩq+1(M),HdRq​(M)≅Hq.​
(54)
The last isomorphism sends a harmonic differential form to its de Rham cohomology class: every class has exactly one harmonic representative. Out-of-range degree spaces are zero.
We first justify the analytic facts needed in the proof. In local coordinates and a smooth frame for the form bundle, the principal symbol of Δq​ is gijξi​ξj​I. This follows from the exterior/contraction identities for d and δ. Freezing the leading coefficients, the Fourier transform estimate for the constant positive quadratic form gives, for each nonnegative integer s,
∥u∥Hs+2​≤Cs​(∥Δq​u∥Hs​+∥u∥L2​).
(55)
Here is how to pass to variable coefficients. On a sufficiently small coordinate ball the difference of leading coefficients has arbitrarily small supremum norm. After differentiating s times, its top-order contribution is bounded by ε∥u∥Hs+2​; derivatives of the coefficients and first-order terms contribute Cs​∥u∥Hs+1​. A partition of unity gives the same types of terms from commutators with the cutoffs. Absorb the epsilon term and use Sobolev interpolation to absorb ∥u∥Hs+1​ into a small multiple of ∥u∥Hs+2​ plus C∥u∥2​. This proves the estimate.
The first-order energy form Q(u,u)=∥du∥22​+∥δu∥22​ satisfies Q(u,u)+c∥u∥22​≥c′∥u∥H12​ for a sufficiently large c>0. This follows from the same frozen-symbol argument at first order, or by integrating the principal part and absorbing the lower-order terms. The Lax-Milgram theorem thus constructs a bounded inverse R=(Δq​+c)−1:L2→H1 in the weak sense. To obtain H2 regularity of this weak solution, use a local difference quotient δh​u and test the weak equation with −δ−h​(χ2δh​u). Positivity of gij bounds ∥χδh​∇u∥22​; derivatives of χ and difference quotients of the smooth coefficients give terms bounded by C∥u∥H1​∥χδh​∇u∥2​ and C∥u∥H12​. The forcing contributes at most C∥f∥2​(∥χδh​∇u∥2​+∥u∥H1​). Absorption gives a bound independent of h, so the difference-quotient criterion yields u∈H2. Differentiating the equation and repeating gives the higher estimates and smoothness for smooth forcing. Thus the use of elliptic regularity here has been justified rather than assumed.
The inverse R is compact as an L2 operator by the Rellich-Kondrachov compactness theorem, and self-adjoint by symmetry of the weak energy form. It is positive and injective with dense range. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators now gives an orthonormal eigenbasis of Δq​, with nonnegative eigenvalues tending to infinity. Each eigenfunction is smooth by the estimates above. In particular Hq is finite-dimensional and there is a positive gap above its zero eigenvalue.
Let Hq​ be the orthogonal projection onto Hq. Define the Green operator of the Hodge Laplacian by multiplying a positive-eigenvalue coefficient by 1/λ and sending the zero coefficients to zero. The gap makes this bounded on L2, and the elliptic estimate shows it maps Hs to Hs+2; hence it sends smooth forms to smooth forms. It obeys
Δq​Gq​=Gq​Δq​=I−Hq​.
(56)
For a smooth q-form α, expand the left side to obtain
α=Hq​α+dδGq​α+δdGq​α.
(57)
These three summands are mutually orthogonal. The energy identity
⟨Δq​h,h⟩=∥dh∥22​+∥δh∥22​
(58)
shows that a harmonic differential form has both dh=0 and δh=0, making it orthogonal to the exact and coexact summands by integration by parts. Also ⟨dβ,δγ⟩=⟨d2β,γ⟩=0. This proves the claimed direct sum and its uniqueness.
Finally let dα=0 and write u=Gq​α. We have dΔq​u=Δq+1​du because d2=0. Since d(α−Hq​α)=0, du is harmonic. It is also exact, so its orthogonality to harmonic forms gives du=0. The decomposition therefore reduces to α=Hq​α+dδu: every closed differential form is cohomologous to a harmonic one. If a harmonic h is exact, h=dβ, then ∥h∥22​=⟨δh,β⟩=0. Hence its class is zero only when h=0, establishing the isomorphism with de Rham cohomology.

a OurBigBook.com
The Gauss lemma says that, for v,w∈Tp​M for which the exponential map is defined,
⟨(dexpp​)v​v,(dexpp​)v​w⟩expp​(v)​=⟨v,w⟩p​.​
(59)
In particular radial and angular directions are orthogonal, and the radial direction retains its length.
Take the variation through geodesics α(t,s)=expp​(t(v+sw)), and put T=∂t​α, J=∂s​α. The Levi-Civita connection is metric compatible and torsion-free, so ∇t​J=∇s​T. Each t-curve is a geodesic, hence ∇t​T=0, and its constant squared speed is ∣v+sw∣p2​. Therefore
dtd​⟨T,J⟩=⟨T,∇t​J⟩=⟨T,∇s​T⟩=21​∂s​∣T∣2=⟨v+sw,w⟩p​.
(60)
At t=0 the variation starts at the fixed point p, so J(0,s)=0. Integrating from 0 to 1 and setting s=0 gives the displayed identity, because T(1,0)=(dexpp​)v​v and J(1,0)=(dexpp​)v​w.
In geodesic normal coordinates based on an orthonormal basis at p, choose v=x and w to be the jth coordinate vector. The lemma gives
gij​(x)xi=xj​,gij(x)xi​=xj​​.
(61)
These identities also hold at x=0 by continuity. They are the radial identities required in part (b).

Use aij=gij, r2=∣x∣2, and E=x⋅∇. The Gauss lemma from part (a) gives
aijxi​=xj​,aijxi​xj​=r2,∑i,j​∂j​(aijxi​)=n.
(62)
For the Gaussian qt​(x)=(4πt)−n/2e−r2/(4t), we have ∂i​qt​=−xi​qt​/(2t). Applying precisely the divergence-form operator in the paper yields
Lqt​=−∂j​(aij∂i​qt​)=2t1​∂j​(xj​qt​)=(2tn​−4t2r2​)qt​.
(63)
Since ∂t​qt​=(−n/(2t)+r2/(4t2))qt​, the Gaussian itself already satisfies (∂t​+L)qt​=0.
For completeness, the product rule gives for an arbitrary smooth G,
(∂t​+L)(qt​G)=qt​(∂t​G+LG+t1​EG).
(64)
Indeed the cross term in L(qt​G) is −2aij(∂i​qt​)(∂j​G)=qt​EG/t. Substituting the formal power series G=∑k≥0​tkBk​, with B0​=1, gives the radial transport equations
(E+k)Bk​=−LBk−1​,k≥1.
(65)
Along a radial segment their unique smooth solution is
Bk​(x)=−∫01​sk−1(LBk−1​)(sx)ds.
(66)
The integral is smooth including at the centre, since each derivative adds a nonnegative power of s to the integrable factor sk−1. Uniqueness follows because a homogeneous solution h has d(skh(sx))/ds=0; smoothness makes its limit at s=0 zero, so h(x)=0. This also excludes singular ray-dependent homogeneous solutions.
Here L1=0, so the recursion successively gives Bk​=0 (k≥1),G(x,t)=1​. Thus both existence and uniqueness hold, with no convergence issue because the formal solution is the exact Gaussian. This is the normal-coordinate divergence-form heat parametrix. The positive Laplace-Beltrami operator −ρ−1∂j​(ρgij∂i​), where ρ=detg​, has an additional first-order term and a different leading amplitude; it is essential to use the operator actually specified here.

c OurBigBook.com
We use a closed manifold of positive dimension n. The nonnegative positive Laplace-Beltrami operator on functions is
Δ=d∗d=−ρ−1∂i​(ρgij∂j​),ρ=det(gij​)​.​
(67)
It satisfies ⟨Δf,f⟩=∫M​∣df∣g2​dvolg​. Its domain as a self-adjoint operator on L2(M) is H2(M). The analytic argument in Question 4(d), with q=0, gives a smooth orthonormal eigenbasis and ordered eigenvalues 0=λ0​≤λ1​≤⋯→∞.
We prove a quantitative counting bound from local Fourier series, rather than assume a spectral asymptotic formula. Choose a finite coordinate cover and smooth functions χα​ compactly supported in its charts with ∑α​χα2​=1. This can be obtained by normalizing an ordinary nonnegative partition of unity by the square root of the sum of its squares. Embed each chart support in a fixed coordinate torus, and extend vα​=χα​f by zero there. Uniform comparison of the coordinate and metric norms, and differentiation of the cutoffs, give constants independent of f such that
c∥f∥22​≤∑α​∥vα​∥L2(Tn)2​,∑α​∥vα​∥H1(Tn)2​≤C(∥df∥22​+∥f∥22​).
(68)
Let PR​ retain the Fourier modes ∣k∣≤R. Parseval identity gives
∥(I−PR​)v∥22​≤R−2∥v∥H12​(R≥1).
(69)
The map f↦(PR​vα​)α​ has target dimension at most C0​Rn, since there are at most Cn​Rn lattice points in each cutoff ball.
Let EΛ​ span all eigenfunctions with eigenvalues at most Λ. For f∈EΛ​, ∥df∥22​≤Λ∥f∥22​. If every retained local coefficient vanishes, the preceding estimates imply
c∥f∥22​≤CR−2(1+Λ)∥f∥22​.
(70)
Choose R=b1+Λ​ with fixed b sufficiently large. Then this is impossible unless f=0, so the finite-dimensional coefficient map is injective on EΛ​. Therefore the eigenvalue counting function satisfies
N(Λ):=dimEΛ​≤C1​(1+Λ)n/2.
(71)
Taking Λ=λk​ gives k+1≤C1​(1+λk​)n/2, so λk​≥c1​(k+1)2/n−1. For all sufficiently large k, this implies λk​≥A0​k2/n.
If M is connected, the zero eigenvalue is simple: Δf=0 implies df=0, hence f is constant. Thus every λk​ for k≥1 is positive. Taking the minimum of A0​ and the finitely many positive ratios λk​/k2/n below the large-k threshold proves
λk​≥Ak2/n(k≥0),A>0.​
(72)
Connectedness is implicit in the printed claim. If M has b>1 connected components, zero has multiplicity b, and the claim fails already at k=1. The same proof gives λk​≥Amax{k−b+1,0}2/n for all k, as well as the universal counting bound above. These finite initial zero modes do not affect part (d).

d OurBigBook.com
Let (ϕj​) be a smooth orthonormal eigenbasis of the positive Laplace-Beltrami operator, with eigenvalues (λj​). The orthonormal eigenbasis defines
e−tΔf=∑j​e−tλj​⟨f,ϕj​⟩ϕj​.
(73)
The large-j lower bound of part (c), valid also after the finitely many zero modes of a disconnected compact manifold, gives λj​≥aj2/n for sufficiently large j. Hence
∑j​e−tλj​<∞(t>0),
(74)
by comparison with ∫0∞​e−tax2/ndx. The operator is positive and diagonal with these summable coefficients, so it is a trace-class operator and its operator trace is their sum.
Its proposed heat kernel is
Kt​(x,y)=∑j​e−tλj​ϕj​(x)ϕj​(y)​.
(75)
We verify smoothness and the kernel action. The elliptic regularity estimate established in Question 4(d) gives, by induction,
∥ϕj​∥H2r​≤Cr​(1+λj​)r.
(76)
The Sobolev embedding theorem therefore gives, for every derivative order a, constants Ca​, ra​ with ∥ϕj​∥Ca​≤Ca​(1+λj​)ra​. Every differentiated term of the kernel series is bounded by Ca,b​e−tλj​(1+λj​)ra​+rb​. An exponential absorbs any fixed power: for t≥τ>0 this is at most Ca,b,τ​e−τλj​/2, a summable bound. Time derivatives merely introduce more powers of λj​. Thus the series converges uniformly with all spatial and time derivatives on [τ,∞)×M×M. In particular Kt​ is smooth for every t>0.
Integrating its uniformly convergent series against f∈L2(M) is legitimate since the compact manifold has finite volume and L2(M)⊆L1(M). It gives exactly the spectral expression above, so
(e−tΔf)(x)=∫M​Kt​(x,y)f(y)dvolg​(y).
(77)
Finally Kt​(x,x)=∑j​e−tλj​∣ϕj​(x)∣2 is nonnegative. Integrating term by term, either by uniform convergence or by Tonelli theorem, and using ∥ϕj​∥2​=1 proves the heat kernel trace formula
Tre−tΔ=j∑​e−tλj​=∫M​Kt​(x,x)dvolg​(x),t>0.​
(78)
